title: NoSQL systems
lead: Scaling through sharding and replication, CAP, BASE and NoSQL data models.

sections.title: Motivation, sharding and replication
sections.html:
Large web workloads motivate horizontal scaling and simpler operations with less cross-node coordination. Sharding partitions data and work; replication creates copies that can serve reads or survive a node failure.

Sharding can make multi-partition reads and transactions expensive. Replication requires propagating writes and deciding what reads observe while copies differ. More machines do not remove these coordination requirements.

NoSQL describes a family of systems, not one fixed consistency or transaction model. Flexible schemas and restricted access patterns can simplify distribution, but the guarantees must be checked for the particular system and operation.

PDF pp. 1–8

sections.title: CAP theorem
sections.html:
CAP concerns the incompatibility of linearizable consistency and availability during a network partition. Consistency here means operations behave like one copy respecting real-time order; it is different from ACID consistency about valid database states.

Availability in the theorem requires operations at nonfailed nodes to complete under its specification. Returning an arbitrary error for every request is not enough to satisfy the intended data-service guarantee. A partition prevents some nodes from communicating reliably.

During a partition, serving an isolated read can return stale data, while waiting for coordination can sacrifice availability. The common “choose any two” triangle is a simplification; guarantees must be stated for the actual failure and operation model.

PDF pp. 9–10

sections.title: BASE and key-value/column-family models
sections.html:
BASE abbreviates basically available, soft state and eventual consistency. Eventual convergence requires updates to stop or settle and the replication/conflict-resolution mechanism to deliver and reconcile outstanding changes. It does not specify a fixed maximum staleness bound.

A key-value model addresses an opaque value by key, commonly with get, put and delete. Hashing can determine shard and replica placement. The application must understand the read/write consistency guarantees.

Column-family models organise sparse, wide records by row keys and column families. They are distinct from the analytical columnar physical layout studied earlier. The source’s system names illustrate categories rather than universal guarantees shared by every product.

PDF pp. 11–14

sections.title: Documents and semi-structured data
sections.html:
A document store exposes the structure of values, allowing predicates on nested fields rather than only lookup by outer key. Documents can contain objects, arrays and scalar values.

JSON represents objects as key-value collections and arrays as ordered value sequences. Documents can differ in their fields, but applications still rely on structural expectations, validation and indexing choices. Flexible schema does not mean data has no structure.

The source contrasts relational tables with nested semi-structured documents. These are logical-model differences; actual storage may use binary representations, and relational engines can also expose JSON operations.

PDF pp. 15–17

sections.title: Graphs and workload-driven choice
sections.html:
A property graph represents entities as nodes, relationships as edges and attributes as properties. Queries can describe graph patterns, traversals, connectivity or paths. The source introduces GQL, SQL/PGQ, Cypher and SPARQL as languages associated with graph querying, with distinct data models and syntax.

Choosing a system requires specifying the required queries, update patterns, transaction boundaries, scale and failure behaviour. A graph model is useful when relationships and traversals are central; documents suit nested aggregates; key-value access suits direct lookup patterns.

SQL and NoSQL capabilities overlap: relational systems can store documents, and some NoSQL systems provide transactions. Evaluate concrete guarantees rather than inferring them from the category label or popularity chart.

PDF pp. 18–21

quiz.question: Two replicas cannot communicate, and one has acknowledged a new write. What is the problem if a later read at the other replica immediately returns the old value?
options: It does not preserve linearizable consistency.
It cannot be a NoSQL system.
quiz.explanation: A read that starts after a successful write but returns the old value does not satisfy linearizability. This is the central trade-off illustrated by CAP.

source.summary: Lecture 27 covers the motivation for NoSQL, sharding and replication, CAP and BASE, data models, and workload-driven choices. This learning material also explains how to interpret simplified CAP diagrams carefully.
